chapters.1.lds: The selected lesson studies comfort received and shared during trials. Why does Paul end his travel explanation by refusing control over their faith?
chapters.1.summary: Paul and Timothy write to the assembly at Corinth and the saints in Achaia. Paul blesses God, who comforts them in every affliction. That comfort lets them comfort others. In Asia they were burdened beyond their strength and expected to die. God delivered them, and the Corinthians helped by prayer. Paul then explains why he changed his travel plan. He was not saying yes and no, for God’s promises are yes in Christ. He stayed away to spare them.
chapters.2.lds: The selected lesson teaches forgiveness as a gift both given and received. Why must sufficient punishment give way to comfort and confirmed love?
chapters.2.summary: Paul decided not to make another painful visit. He wrote a letter instead, with many tears. He says someone has caused sorrow to the whole assembly. The punishment given by the majority is enough. Now they should forgive and comfort the man and confirm their love. Paul forgives whomever they forgive, so Satan gains no advantage. At Troas a door opened, but Paul went on to Macedonia to find Titus. He thanks God, who spreads the knowledge of Christ like a fragrance.
chapters.3.lds: How can the believers themselves function as a recommendation letter?
chapters.3.summary: Paul asks if he needs letters of recommendation, as some do. He says the Corinthians are his letter, known and read by all. His sufficiency is from God, who made him a servant of a new covenant. The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life. The service written on stones came with glory, and Moses’ face shone. The service of the Spirit has greater glory. Moses veiled his face, and Paul says a veil remains when Moses is read. When someone turns to the Lord, the veil is taken away.
chapters.4.lds: The selected lesson studies hope and comfort during trials. Why does Paul compare powerful treasure with fragile clay carriers?
chapters.4.summary: Paul says he does not lose heart in this service. He refuses hidden and shameful ways and does not twist God’s word. If the good news is veiled, it is veiled to those who are perishing. God has shone in hearts to give the light of his glory in Christ’s face. This treasure is held in clay vessels. Paul is pressed, perplexed, pursued, and struck down, yet not destroyed. He carries Jesus’ death in his body so that Jesus’ life may show. The outward person decays, but the inward is renewed daily.
chapters.5.lds: The selected lesson teaches restored relationship with God through Jesus Christ’s Atonement. How does restored relationship change the purpose of the speakers’ appeal?
chapters.5.summary: Paul calls the body an earthly tent and expects a building from God. He groans to be clothed with it, and the Spirit is the pledge. He walks by faith, not by sight, and aims to please the Lord. All must appear before Christ’s judgment seat. Christ’s love compels him, because one died for all. So he no longer regards anyone by human measure. Anyone in Christ is a new creation. God was reconciling the world in Christ, and Paul begs them to be reconciled.
chapters.6.lds: Why does Paul pair sorrow with joy and poverty with riches?
chapters.6.summary: Paul urges them not to receive God’s grace in vain. He says now is the day of salvation. He commends himself by endurance in beatings, prisons, riots, labor, and hunger. He is called a deceiver yet is true, and is poor yet enriches many. He says his heart is wide open to the Corinthians. Any narrowness is in their own feelings. He asks them to open their hearts in return. Then he warns against being yoked with unbelievers, for they are God’s temple.
chapters.7.lds: The selected lesson teaches sorrow that leads to repentance and changed conduct. Why does Paul value changed conduct rather than sorrow by itself?
chapters.7.summary: Paul asks the Corinthians to make room for him. In Macedonia he had fights outside and fears inside. God comforted him by the coming of Titus. Titus reported their longing, mourning, and zeal for Paul. Paul’s earlier letter grieved them, and for a while he regretted it. Now he rejoices, because their grief led to repentance. Godly sorrow brings repentance, but the world’s sorrow brings death. Titus was refreshed by them, and Paul’s boast about them proved true.
chapters.8.lds: The selected lesson teaches sharing with people in need. How do chosen companions protect the collection from blame?
chapters.8.summary: Paul tells of the grace given to the assemblies of Macedonia. In deep poverty they gave beyond their means for the saints. He urges the Corinthians to finish the gift they began a year ago. He points to Christ, who was rich and became poor for them. A gift is accepted according to what a person has. The aim is equality, as with the manna. Titus goes to them willingly, with two brothers. Paul takes care that no one can blame how the money is handled.
chapters.9.lds: The selected lesson teaches cheerful giving rather than reluctant action. Why does advance preparation help protect giving from pressure?
chapters.9.summary: Paul has boasted to the Macedonians that Achaia was ready a year ago. He sends the brothers ahead so the gift is ready when he comes. He does not want it to look forced. One who sows sparingly reaps sparingly. Each should give as he has decided, for God loves a cheerful giver. God is able to supply them for every good work. The gift meets the saints’ needs and causes many thanks to God. Paul ends by thanking God for his unspeakable gift.
chapters.10.lds: How does authority’s purpose limit its use against the hearers?
chapters.10.summary: Paul appeals to them by the meekness and gentleness of Christ. Some say he is humble in person and bold only when away. He says his weapons are not of the flesh but can pull down strongholds. They say his letters are weighty, but his presence is weak. He answers that he will be the same in deed when present. He will not compare himself with those who commend themselves. He boasts only within the field God gave him, which reaches Corinth. The one the Lord commends is approved.
chapters.11.lds: The selected lesson teaches a simple focus on following Jesus Christ. Why does Paul’s boasting list so many dangers and weaknesses?
chapters.11.summary: Paul asks them to bear with a little foolishness. He fears they will be led astray, as the serpent deceived Eve. He taught them free of charge, and other assemblies supported him. He calls his rivals false apostles. Then he boasts as a fool. He lists labors, prisons, beatings, shipwrecks, dangers, hunger, and cold. Besides these he carries daily concern for all the assemblies. He ends with his escape from Damascus in a basket through the wall.
chapters.12.lds: The selected lesson teaches finding strength through the Savior’s grace within weakness. How does the answer about grace differ from Paul’s requested removal?
chapters.12.summary: Paul tells of a man caught up to paradise, who heard unspeakable words. He will boast of that man but of himself only in weaknesses. A thorn in the flesh was given to him to keep him from pride. Three times he asked the Lord to remove it. The Lord answered that his grace is sufficient. So Paul takes pleasure in weaknesses, for when he is weak he is strong. He says he was no burden to them and will come a third time. He fears he may find quarrels and sin not repented of.
chapters.13.lds: Why does Paul pray for right conduct even if he appears to fail?
chapters.13.summary: Paul says this will be his third visit. Every matter will be settled by two or three witnesses. He warns that he will not spare those who sinned before. Christ was crucified in weakness and lives by God’s power. He tells them to test themselves, whether they are in the faith. He prays that they do no evil, even if he seems to have failed. He closes with a call to rejoice, agree, and live in peace. The last line names Christ’s grace, God’s love, and the Spirit’s fellowship.
